subChunks.title: JUnit 5 Fundamentals
subChunks.hookHtml: An untested spell is a gamble. JUnit 5 gives you the alchemy table to verify every incantation works exactly as intended — before it fires in the field. Master the anatomy of a test and your code becomes provably correct.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Anatomy of a JUnit 5 Test Class

Every test class follows a clear structure: lifecycle annotations control setup and teardown; @Test marks each test method; assertions verify behaviour.

import org.junit.jupiter.api.*;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.*;

class CalculatorTest {

    Calculator calculator; // the system under test

    @BeforeAll
    static void initAll() {
        System.out.println("Runs ONCE before all tests in the class");
    }

    @BeforeEach
    void setUp() {
        calculator = new Calculator(); // fresh instance before EACH test
    }

    @AfterEach
    void tearDown() {
        // cleanup after each test
    }

    @AfterAll
    static void tearDownAll() {
        System.out.println("Runs ONCE after all tests in the class");
    }

    @Test
    @DisplayName("Adding two positive numbers returns correct sum")
    void testAdd() {
        int result = calculator.add(3, 7);
        assertEquals(10, result, "3 + 7 should equal 10");
    }
}

Core Assertions

JUnit 5 assertions are in org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions. Each accepts an optional message as the last argument shown when the assertion fails.

assertEquals(expected, actual);          // values are equal
assertNotEquals(unexpected, actual);     // values are NOT equal
assertTrue(condition);                   // condition is true
assertFalse(condition);                  // condition is false
assertNull(object);                      // object is null
assertNotNull(object);                   // object is not null

// assertThrows — verifies an exception is thrown
assertThrows(ArithmeticException.class, () -> calculator.divide(10, 0));

// assertAll — runs ALL assertions even if some fail (grouped assertions)
assertAll("Calculator assertions",
    () -> assertEquals(5,  calculator.add(2, 3)),
    () -> assertEquals(10, calculator.add(4, 6)),
    () -> assertEquals(0,  calculator.add(-1, 1))
);

// assertTimeout — fails if execution exceeds the duration
assertTimeout(Duration.ofMillis(100), () -> calculator.add(1, 2));

Parameterized Tests

Rather than writing a separate test for each input, @ParameterizedTest runs the same test logic with multiple inputs. This dramatically reduces duplication.

@ParameterizedTest
@ValueSource(ints = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5})
void addingOneAlwaysIncrementsBy1(int value) {
    assertEquals(value + 1, calculator.add(value, 1));
}

// CsvSource for multiple parameters:
@ParameterizedTest
@CsvSource({"2, 3, 5", "10, 20, 30", "-1, 1, 0"})
void add_withMultipleInputs(int a, int b, int expected) {
    assertEquals(expected, calculator.add(a, b));
}

Nested Tests for Organisation

@Nested allows grouping related tests in inner classes, with their own lifecycle annotations. Tests in a nested class can also share a different state setup from the outer class.

class CalculatorTest {
    @Nested
    @DisplayName("Division tests")
    class DivisionTests {
        @Test
        void dividePositiveNumbers() { assertEquals(5, calculator.divide(10, 2)); }

        @Test
        void divideByZeroThrows() {
            assertThrows(ArithmeticException.class, () -> calculator.divide(1, 0));
        }
    }

    @Nested
    @DisplayName("Addition tests")
    class AdditionTests {
        @Test
        void addPositiveNumbers() { assertEquals(5, calculator.add(3, 2)); }
    }
}

Test Lifecycle and Best Practices

Each @Test method should be independent — no shared mutable state between tests. Use @BeforeEach to reset state rather than relying on test ordering. Follow the AAA pattern: Arrange (set up inputs), Act (call the method), Assert (verify the output). Tests should be FIRST: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely.

@Test
@DisplayName("Divide returns correct quotient for positive inputs")
void testDivide_positiveInputs() {
    // Arrange
    int dividend = 10;
    int divisor  = 2;

    // Act
    int result = calculator.divide(dividend, divisor);

    // Assert
    assertEquals(5, result);
}

storyBeats.text: After years of crafting spells, Archmage Eldrin instituted a sacred law: no spell leaves the workshop without passing the Trial Chamber. Every incantation must be verified, every edge case proven harmless.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: A test is a contract. It states: given these inputs, this method must produce this output. Break the contract and the build fails — protecting everyone who relies on your code.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: @BeforeEach resets the world before every trial. No test should inherit the mess of the previous one. Each @Test begins with a clean slate — that is independence.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: @ParameterizedTest is the batch trial — run the same verification against a dozen inputs without writing a dozen test methods. Data-driven testing, the mark of a thorough mage.

storyBeats.speaker: Parameterized Test

storyBeats.text: The Trial Chamber hummed with efficiency. Dozens of spells verified in seconds, each test isolated, each edge case covered. The Academy's spellbook was now provably correct — a luxury most wizards never knew they needed.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
In the text editor below, write a complete JUnit 5 test class for a SpellCalculator service with these methods:

  • int add(int a, int b) — returns the sum
  • int divide(int a, int b) — returns the quotient; throws ArithmeticException if b is 0

Your test class must include:

  1. At least 2 @Test methods with @DisplayName, following the AAA (Arrange/Act/Assert) pattern
  2. A test using assertThrows for divide-by-zero
  3. A @ParameterizedTest with @CsvSource covering at least 3 input/output combinations for add()
  4. A @BeforeEach method that creates a fresh SpellCalculator before each test
  5. An assertAll grouping at least 2 related assertions

Focus on completeness and correctness of the test structure — the code does not run in the sandbox, so express your understanding through well-formed test code.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between @BeforeEach and @BeforeAll — when would you use each? Why is test independence important, and how does @BeforeEach enforce it? What is the advantage of @ParameterizedTest over writing separate test methods for each input case?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Without looking at the reference code, write a complete JUnit 5 test class for a SpellCalculator with add() and divide() methods. Your answer should include: @BeforeEach setup, at least 2 @Test methods with @DisplayName and AAA pattern, an assertThrows test for divide-by-zero, a @ParameterizedTest with @CsvSource, and at least one assertAll group. Write it out from memory, demonstrating your understanding of each annotation's purpose.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Arrange-Act-Assert: the standard structure for test methods. Arrange sets up inputs and state, Act calls the method under test, Assert verifies the outcome. Keeps tests readable and focused.

Good tests are: Fast (run in milliseconds), Independent (no dependency on other tests), Repeatable (same result every run), Self-validating (pass or fail — no manual inspection), Timely (written alongside production code).
JUnit 5 extension mechanism. @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) enables Mockito's @Mock injection. @ExtendWith(SpringExtension.class) enables Spring context. Replaces JUnit 4's @RunWith.

assertThrows() returns the thrown exception, allowing you to make further assertions on it: var ex = assertThrows(ArithmeticException.class, () -> ...); assertEquals("Division by zero", ex.getMessage());
Tests must not share mutable state — each must set up its own environment. Shared state causes 'test pollution' where one test's side effects make another test fail or pass incorrectly.
Temporarily disables a test or entire class without deleting it. Useful while debugging, but should be removed — disabled tests don't protect your code.

JUnit 5 = JUnit Platform (test runner/launcher) + JUnit Jupiter (new API, the @Test annotations) + JUnit Vintage (JUnit 3/4 compatibility). jupiter is what you write; platform is what IDEs and build tools use.
TDD: write the test first (it fails — RED), write minimal code to make it pass (GREEN), then refactor while keeping tests green (REFACTOR). Produces testable, well-designed code by necessity.

options: @BeforeEach runs once before the entire test class; @BeforeAll runs before each test method
@BeforeEach runs before each individual test method; @BeforeAll runs once before all tests in the class and must be static
They are identical — both run before each test
@BeforeAll only works with @Nested test classes
questions.correctAnswer: @BeforeEach runs before each individual test method; @BeforeAll runs once before all tests in the class and must be static
questions.explanationHtml: @BeforeEach ensures a fresh setup before every single test (important for independence). @BeforeAll runs once for the entire class — use it for expensive one-time setup (e.g., starting a database). @BeforeAll methods must be static (unless using @TestInstance(PER_CLASS)).

questions.questionHtml: You want to verify that divide(10, 0) throws an ArithmeticException. Which assertion is correct?
options: assertEquals(ArithmeticException.class, calculator.divide(10, 0))
assertTrue(calculator.divide(10, 0) throws ArithmeticException)
assertThrows(ArithmeticException.class, () -> calculator.divide(10, 0))
assertException(ArithmeticException.class, calculator.divide(10, 0))
questions.explanationHtml: assertThrows(ExceptionType.class, executable) is the correct JUnit 5 way to verify that an exception is thrown. The executable is a lambda that calls the code expected to throw. It also returns the exception for further assertions.

questions.questionHtml: This test is fragile — it sometimes fails when run with other tests. What is the likely cause?
questions.correctAnswer: Shared static mutable state (runCount) is modified by tests, causing ordering-dependent failures. Use @BeforeEach to reset state instead.
questions.explanationHtml: Shared mutable static state breaks test independence. runCount's value depends on which tests ran previously and in what order. Fix: move state to instance fields, initialise in @BeforeEach, and remove the static modifier. Each test then starts with a clean, predictable state.

questions.questionHtml: When is assertAll() preferable over multiple separate assertEquals() calls?
options: assertAll() is always faster than multiple assertEquals() calls
When you want ALL assertions to be evaluated and reported even if earlier ones fail — giving a complete failure picture in one run
When testing a single value against multiple types
assertAll() automatically retries failed assertions
questions.correctAnswer: When you want ALL assertions to be evaluated and reported even if earlier ones fail — giving a complete failure picture in one run
questions.explanationHtml: With separate assertEquals() calls, the first failure stops the test — you fix it, re-run, and discover the next failure. assertAll() evaluates all assertions and reports every failure at once, giving you the complete picture in a single test run — much more efficient for multi-field validation.

subChunks.title: Mockito: Mocking Dependencies
subChunks.hookHtml: Your SpellService calls a SpellRepository — but the database isn't running in tests. Mockito conjures fake implementations that behave exactly as you specify, letting you test your service logic in pure isolation.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Mocks, Stubs, and Spies — The Vocabulary

These terms are often confused. A stub returns canned answers to calls; a mock additionally verifies that expected calls were made; a spy wraps a real object, delegating to it by default but allowing selective stubbing and verification.

// Stub: returns a value; no verification of interaction
when(repo.findByName("Fireball")).thenReturn(Optional.of(spell));

// Mock: returns a value AND you verify calls happened
when(repo.findByName("Fireball")).thenReturn(Optional.of(spell));
verify(repo).findByName("Fireball"); // verifies the call was made

// Spy: real object with selective overrides
SpellRepository spy = Mockito.spy(new RealSpellRepository());
doReturn(Optional.of(spell)).when(spy).findByName("Fireball");

Setting Up Mockito with JUnit 5

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) enables automatic mock injection via annotations. @Mock creates a mock implementation of an interface or class. @InjectMocks creates the system under test and injects all @Mock fields into it.

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class SpellServiceTest {

    @Mock
    SpellRepository spellRepository; // Mockito creates a fake implementation

    @InjectMocks
    SpellService spellService; // SpellService receives the mock via constructor or field injection

    @Test
    void findSpell_returnsSpellFromRepository() {
        Spell expectedSpell = new Spell("Fireball", 90);

        // Stubbing: when repo.findByName is called with "Fireball", return expectedSpell
        when(spellRepository.findByName("Fireball"))
            .thenReturn(Optional.of(expectedSpell));

        // Act
        Optional<Spell> result = spellService.findSpell("Fireball");

        // Assert
        assertTrue(result.isPresent());
        assertEquals("Fireball", result.get().getName());

        // Verify the interaction occurred exactly once
        verify(spellRepository, times(1)).findByName("Fireball");
    }
}

Stubbing with when().thenReturn() and Variants

Mockito's stubbing API is expressive. Chain methods for richer behaviour.

// Return different values on consecutive calls
when(repo.findAll())
    .thenReturn(List.of(spell1))   // first call
    .thenReturn(List.of(spell2));  // second call

// Throw an exception
when(repo.save(any())).thenThrow(new RuntimeException("DB down"));

// Stubbing void methods (can't use when() — it returns nothing)
doNothing().when(repo).delete(anyString());
doThrow(new RuntimeException()).when(repo).delete("forbidden");

// Argument matchers — match any argument
when(repo.findByName(anyString())).thenReturn(Optional.empty());
when(repo.findByPower(gt(50))).thenReturn(List.of(powerfulSpell));

Verifying Interactions

verify() asserts that a method was called on a mock with specific arguments. Combine with times(), never(), atLeastOnce(), atMost(n) for precise interaction verification.

verify(repo).findByName("Fireball");           // called exactly once
verify(repo, times(3)).findByName(any());      // called exactly 3 times
verify(repo, never()).delete(anyString());     // never called
verify(repo, atLeastOnce()).findAll();         // called at least once

// Verify no more interactions happened
verifyNoMoreInteractions(spellRepository);

// Verify nothing was called at all
verifyNoInteractions(spellRepository);

When NOT to Mock

Mocks should represent dependencies that are external, slow, or non-deterministic (databases, HTTP APIs, file system, random/time). Do NOT mock: value objects (records, POJOs), static utility methods, or the class under test itself. Over-mocking leads to tests that verify implementation details rather than behaviour — they break when you refactor internals without changing observable outputs.

// WRONG: mocking a simple value object
Spell spell = mock(Spell.class); // unnecessary — just use new Spell("X", 10)

// RIGHT: mocking an external dependency
SpellRepository repo = mock(SpellRepository.class); // database — external!

storyBeats.text: The Academy's SpellService depended on a mystical repository deep in the dungeon — a database that took seconds to initialise and only worked when the arcane network was online. Testing was impossible. Until Mockito arrived.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Mockito conjures a fake repository — a magical duplicate that behaves however you instruct. Call when().thenReturn() to script its responses, then verify() to ensure your service spoke to it correctly.

storyBeats.speaker: Mockito Setup
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: verify() is the witness statement — it proves the service actually spoke to the repository with the correct arguments. A test that doesn't verify interactions might pass even if the service forgets to call the repository entirely.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: But be warned — mock only what is truly external. A simple value object needs no mock. Over-mocking binds your tests to implementation details, not behaviour. When you refactor, they shatter needlessly.

storyBeats.speaker: Stubbing Void Methods

storyBeats.text: The Trial Chamber ran in milliseconds. No dungeon database, no arcane network required. The mock repositories answered perfectly, the verifications confirmed every interaction, and the SpellService's logic was proven beyond doubt.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
In the text editor, write a complete JUnit 5 + Mockito test class for a SpellService with a SpellRepository dependency. The service has a findSpell(String name) method that delegates to spellRepository.findByName(name).

Your test class must demonstrate:

  1. @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) at class level
  2. @Mock SpellRepository and @InjectMocks SpellService
  3. A test that stubs the repository using when(repo.findByName("Fireball")).thenReturn(...) and asserts the service returns the correct result
  4. verify() that the repository's method was called with the expected argument
  5. A test that stubs the repository to return Optional.empty() and verifies the service handles it gracefully
  6. A test demonstrating doThrow() for simulating a repository failure

Write complete, syntactically correct code demonstrating your understanding of each Mockito concept.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain the difference between a mock and a stub. Why does Mockito have both when().thenReturn() and doReturn().when() syntaxes — when would you use each? What is the risk of using verifyNoMoreInteractions() in every test, and when is it genuinely useful?
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: From memory, write a complete JUnit 5 + Mockito test class with @ExtendWith, @Mock, and @InjectMocks. Write a test that stubs a repository method, calls the service, asserts the result, and verifies the interaction. Include a second test stubbing an empty result and a third demonstrating doThrow() for error scenarios. Focus on demonstrating your understanding of the Mockito API and testing philosophy.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Stub: returns canned answers, no interaction verification. Mock: verifiable stub — you can assert calls were made. Spy: wraps a real object, real behaviour by default with optional overrides. Use mocks for external dependencies, spies rarely, and stubs for simple cases.
Mockito inspects the class under test and injects @Mock fields via constructor injection first, then setter injection, then field injection. Prefer constructor injection for clarity and testability.

Mockito's any(), anyString(), eq(), gt() etc. allow flexible stubbing and verification. Rule: if you use a matcher for one argument, ALL arguments in that call must use matchers — you can't mix matchers and literal values.

A BDD-flavoured Mockito API: given(...).willReturn(...) instead of when(...).thenReturn(...). Reads more naturally as a story: given the repo is configured, when the service is called, then the result should be...
MockitoExtension enables strict stubbing by default (Mockito 2.x+). Unused stubs cause test failures — keeping tests clean and highlighting over-specification.
ArgumentCaptor lets you capture the actual arguments passed to a mock method, then assert on them. Useful when the argument is constructed internally by the code under test.

Gerard Meszaros coined the term 'test double' as the umbrella term for dummies (unused parameters), fakes (working simple implementations), stubs, spies, and mocks. Mockito primarily creates mocks and spies.
Mocking too many things — especially the class under test — leads to tests that pass even when logic is broken. Tests should verify behaviour from the outside, not implementation details.

options: It marks a field as a mock to be created by Mockito
It creates an instance of the class under test and injects all @Mock annotated fields into it
It verifies that all mocked methods were called at least once
It disables strict stubbing for a specific test class
questions.correctAnswer: It creates an instance of the class under test and injects all @Mock annotated fields into it
questions.explanationHtml: @InjectMocks tells Mockito to instantiate the annotated type and inject all @Mock fields into it (via constructor, setter, or field injection). It's the system under test; @Mock fields are its dependencies.

questions.questionHtml: Which code correctly stubs a void method to throw an exception when called?
options: when(repo.delete("x")).thenThrow(new RuntimeException())
doThrow(new RuntimeException()).when(repo).delete("x")
assertThrows(RuntimeException.class, () -> repo.delete("x"))
mockThrow(RuntimeException.class).on(repo.delete("x"))
questions.explanationHtml: Void methods cannot use the when(method()).then... syntax because void methods don't return a value for when() to capture. Use doThrow(exception).when(mock).voidMethod(args) instead.

questions.questionHtml: This test always passes even when the service ignores the repository. What is missing?
questions.correctAnswer: Add verify(spellRepository).findByName("Fireball") to confirm the service actually called the repository
questions.explanationHtml: Without verify(), the test only checks the output, not that the service used the repository. If the service returned a hardcoded result and ignored the repo, the test would still pass. Add verify(spellRepository, times(1)).findByName("Fireball") to confirm the interaction occurred.

questions.questionHtml: When should you NOT use a mock?
options: When testing a class that calls a database
When testing a class that makes HTTP requests
When testing a simple value object or record that has no external dependencies
When testing a class that reads from the file system
questions.correctAnswer: When testing a simple value object or record that has no external dependencies
questions.explanationHtml: Value objects (POJOs, records, simple data holders) have no external dependencies — just create them with new. Mocking them adds complexity without benefit and couples your test to internal structure. Reserve mocks for external, slow, or non-deterministic dependencies (databases, APIs, file systems, clocks).
